name: Mattos v. Agarano (with Brooks v. City of Seattle)
court: Ninth Circuit, en banc (from the District of Hawaii, District Judge David A. Ezra, and the Western District of Washington, District Judge Richard A. Jones)
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, Taser used in drive stun mode three times in under a minute on a pregnant driver who refused to leave her car, and in dart mode without warning on the wife at a domestic call, both held excessive on the plaintiffs' facts, qualified immunity granted because Taser law was not clearly established in 2004 and 2006
summary: Sitting en banc, the Ninth Circuit decided two Taser cases together. In Brooks, Seattle officers drive stunned a seven months pregnant driver three times in less than a minute to remove her from her car after she refused to sign a speeding citation. In Mattos, a Maui officer fired a Taser in dart mode, without warning, at the wife who had called 911 about a domestic dispute when she ended up between the officer and her husband. The court held that a reasonable jury could find both uses excessive, and that the officers were nonetheless entitled to qualified immunity because no case had held a Taser use unconstitutional when the incidents occurred. It is the case that teaches warnings, repeated applications, and the difference between failing to facilitate an arrest and actively resisting it.
coverage: The en banc opinion by Judge Paez, Judge Schroeder's concurrence, Chief Judge Kozinski's partial concurrence and dissent (joined by Judge Bea), Judge Silverman's partial concurrence and dissent (joined by Judge Clifton), and all footnotes were read in full from the Ninth Circuit's archive at https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2011/10/17/08-15567.pdf. The slip opinion carries both docket numbers, 08-15567 and 08-35526, and the district court numbers 07-CV-00220-DAE and 2:06-cv-01681-RAJ.

The slip opinion does not print its own Federal Reporter citation. The citation 661 F.3d 433 is the one given in the course materials and the assignment and could not be confirmed from the source read. The filing date, docket numbers and en banc status are confirmed from the slip opinion.
The withdrawn three judge panel opinions (Mattos v. Agarano, 590 F.3d 1082, and Brooks v. City of Seattle, 599 F.3d 1018) were not read; they are described only as the en banc opinion describes them.

Facts are stated as the en banc court stated them, in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs. Chief Judge Kozinski's dissent recites additional facts favorable to the officers (for example that Jones told Brooks he would use the Taser if she did not leave the car); those are noted in the dissent field, not in the facts.
facts:
Both cases reached the court on interlocutory appeal from denials of qualified immunity, so the facts are the plaintiffs' versions.

Brooks. On November 23, 2004, Malaika Brooks, 33 years old and seven months pregnant, was driving her 11 year old son to school in Seattle when she was stopped for doing 32 miles per hour in a 20 mile per hour school zone. She gave Officer Ornelas her license and sent her son across the street to school. Told she would be cited, she insisted she had not been speeding and refused to sign the citation. Officer Jones explained that signing was not an admission; Brooks called him a liar, and he said she would go to jail if she did not sign. Sergeant Daman arrived, asked once more, and told the officers to book her. Ornelas told her to get out; she refused. Jones displayed a Taser and asked if she knew what it was. She said she did not, and said she was pregnant and less than 60 days from delivery. Jones asked how pregnant. The officers then discussed where to apply it; Brooks heard one say not to do it in her stomach but in her thigh. Ornelas opened the door and twisted her arm behind her back; she stiffened and clutched the steering wheel. Jones cycled the Taser to show her. Ornelas got the keys out of the ignition and they fell to the floor. Twenty-seven seconds after the demonstration, Jones applied the Taser in drive stun mode to her left thigh. She cried and honked the horn. Thirty-six seconds later he applied it to her left arm, and six seconds after that to her neck. She fell over, was dragged out, laid face down in the street and handcuffed. She was convicted of refusing to sign the citation; a jury hung on resisting arrest. Her daughter was born healthy. Brooks has permanent burn scars.

Mattos. On August 23, 2006, after a domestic dispute, Jayzel Mattos had her 14 year old daughter call police. Officers Agarano, MacKnight and Kunioka found Troy Mattos, six feet three and about 200 pounds, sitting outside the front door smelling of alcohol with open beer bottles nearby. Troy said nothing physical had happened and became agitated. Kunioka asked to speak with Jayzel; Troy went inside to get her and Agarano stepped in behind him, which angered Troy. Agarano asked Jayzel to come outside and she agreed. Before she could, Officer Aikala entered, stood in the living room and announced Troy was under arrest. Jayzel was already standing in front of Troy and did not immediately move. Aikala moved in and pushed against her chest; she extended her arm to keep her breasts from being pressed against him. Aikala asked, "Are you touching an officer?" She was at the same time asking Agarano why Troy was being arrested, urging everyone to calm down and go outside, and asking that her sleeping children not be disturbed. Without warning, Aikala shot her with a Taser in dart mode. She felt a burning pain that locked her joints and muscles and fell hard to the floor. Both spouses were arrested; all charges were later dropped.

In each case the district court denied the officers summary judgment on qualified immunity, a three judge panel reversed, and the full court took the cases en banc and heard them together.
holding:
The court held that both plaintiffs alleged Fourth Amendment violations but that the officers were entitled to qualified immunity on the section 1983 claims because the law was not clearly established at the time. In Brooks it affirmed the denial of Washington state qualified immunity on the assault and battery claims, because a reasonable jury could find excessive force.

Framework. The court applied Graham through Deorle: first the nature and quality of the intrusion, then the governmental interest measured by the severity of the crime, immediate threat (the most important factor, which requires objective facts rather than a bare statement of fear), active resistance or flight, and any other factors the totality of circumstances makes relevant. On the clearly established prong it applied Ashcroft v. al-Kidd: precedent must place the question beyond debate, courts may not define the law at a high level of generality, and the obvious case exception sets a high bar.

Brooks. The Taser was used in drive stun mode, which delivers a painful shock but does not override the nervous system as dart mode does. The record was insufficient to decide what level of force drive stun is, and the court did not decide it; what mattered was reasonableness, keeping in mind the magnitude of the shock and the extreme pain. Failing to sign a citation and driving 32 in a 20 zone are not serious offenses. Brooks never threatened the officers, gave no sign of being armed, and once the keys were out of the ignition posed not even a potential threat. She did resist arrest by refusing to get out and by stiffening and clutching the wheel, but her resistance was not violent, she did not flee, and there was no exigency; the officers proceeded deliberately, pausing to discuss where to tase her. Two factors the court called overwhelmingly salient: the officers knew she was pregnant and considered it before tasing her, and Jones tased her three times in less than one minute, leaving no time to recover from the pain and reconsider. A reasonable fact finder could conclude the force was unreasonable. On immunity, the only circuit Taser cases in November 2004 (Russo, Hinton and Draper) had rejected excessive force claims, and although each was factually distinguishable, the court could not say every reasonable officer would have understood beyond debate that tasing Brooks was excessive, and Graham alone did not make it obvious.

Mattos. Dart mode is intermediate, significant force under Bryan. Jayzel's offense, if any, was minimal; attempting to keep the officer from pressing against her breasts did not rise to obstruction. She posed no threat: no reason to think she was armed, no verbal threat, and her only contact with Aikala was defensive. On resistance, the court drew a distinction between a failure to facilitate an arrest and active resistance, and noted she was trying to comply with Agarano's request to step outside when she was caught between the two men. The court took seriously the danger of domestic violence calls and accepted that a reasonable officer could be concerned for his safety on arrival, but held that the leeway given officers who enter a home to intervene in a domestic dispute does not extend to using intermediate force on the non-threatening victim they came to protect, especially when the dispute appeared to be over. Jayzel was not culpable for the situation, children were present, and tasing the innocent wife of a large, drunk, angry man when neither spouse was armed was not a prudent way to defuse a potentially, but not yet, dangerous situation. The absence of any warning, when a warning was plausible, pushed the force "far beyond the pale." A reasonable fact finder could conclude the force was excessive. On immunity, in August 2006 there was still no Supreme Court or Ninth Circuit decision on dart mode Tasers and no circuit case finding a Taser use unconstitutional, so the officers were immune.

Disposition: No. 08-15567 reversed; No. 08-35526 reversed in part and affirmed in part.
notDecided:
Whether a Taser in drive stun mode is intermediate force. The court said the record was insufficient and that reasonableness, not the label, controlled.

Whether the officers used excessive force in fact. The court held only that a reasonable jury could so find on the plaintiffs' versions. Brooks's state law assault and battery claims were left to proceed; the Mattoses' federal claim ended with immunity.

Whether the Seattle officers had probable cause to make a custodial arrest. The court held that question did not affect the excessive force analysis.

The warrantless entry and arrest claims in Mattos. The district court had granted summary judgment on them and they were not before the en banc court.

Any per se rule about Taser use. The court stressed there are no per se rules in the Fourth Amendment excessive force context.
inPractice:
Mattos and Brooks are the Ninth Circuit's clearest statement that a Taser is not an answer to non-compliance by itself. In both cases the officers had a lawful reason to act and a subject who was not doing what they said, and in both the court still found the force unreasonable on the plaintiffs' facts. The lesson is not that officers may never tase a resisting arrestee. It is that the reason for the force has to match the force.

From Brooks: repeated applications are their own problem. Three cycles in fifty seconds gave the subject no chance to comply between them, and the court weighed the known pregnancy heavily. The deliberate pause to discuss where to apply the Taser showed the court there was time to think, which undercut any claim of a split second decision. The keys being removed eliminated the only real threat before the first application.

From Mattos: a person who is in the way is not a person who is fighting. The court separated failing to facilitate an arrest from actively resisting it, and it refused to transfer the danger of a domestic call onto the non-threatening victim. The missing warning was decisive language in the opinion. If a warning is plausible, give it.

The immunity rulings closed a window. Both incidents predated Bryan. The court said in substance that the gap in Taser law existed then, and it has not existed since. Officers who rely on Mattos for its immunity holding are relying on the state of the law in 2004 and 2006.

Dr. Sowards teaches these cases with Bryan in the less lethal line: drive stun versus dart mode, warnings, cycle counts, and the passive versus active distinction.
trainIt:
Train cycle discipline. Students should know that each application is a separate use of force that needs its own justification, that the court counted the seconds between applications, and that the subject must be given a realistic chance to comply after each one. Build evaluations that require a verbal command and an observed response between cycles, and require students to say aloud what changed to justify a second application.

Train the warning as a reflex. In Mattos the officer gave none; in Brooks the officer cycled the device as a demonstration, which the court treated as a warning but then weighed against the three rapid applications that followed. A warning is a command, a stated consequence, and time to comply. Train it in dart mode and in drive stun mode.

Teach the known vulnerability factor. The officers in Brooks learned she was seven months pregnant and tased her anyway. Students should treat a disclosed pregnancy, visible age or frailty, or a medical statement as a factor that raises the justification needed, and should be able to explain in a report why force was still necessary if it was.

Teach the domestic call distinction. Scenario: officers arrive at a 911 call from the wife, the husband is large, intoxicated and hostile, and the wife ends up between the officer and the husband. Students must distinguish the threat posed by the husband from the conduct of the wife and must identify what she is actually doing: standing in the way and talking, or fighting. The court drew that line and expects officers to draw it.

Teach the posture. Both cases were decided on the plaintiffs' versions of disputed facts; the court found that a jury could find excessive force and granted immunity only because the law was not clearly established at the time. Students should hear the dissents too, because they show how differently reasonable judges read the same record.
caution: The reporter citation 661 F.3d 433 could not be confirmed from the slip opinion and is taken from the course materials. All facts are stated in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs as required on these interlocutory appeals; the officers' versions differ, and the dissents recite facts (such as a verbal warning to Brooks before the first application) that the majority did not credit at this stage. The court granted qualified immunity on the federal claims in both cases, so neither case produced a liability finding against the officers; the finding that a jury could find excessive force governs only the posture of the cases and the notice it gives for later conduct.
dissent: Chief Judge Kozinski, joined by Judge Bea, concurred in the immunity rulings but would have found no constitutional violation in either case. He wrote that citizens who refuse to comply with police orders breach a covenant of cooperation, that the Taser is a safer alternative to hands-on force, batons and chemical agents, that Brooks was under arrest, wedged into her seat with keys in the car, and that the officers were patient and used the lightest application available; he asked what alternative the majority would have had them use and would have granted state law immunity as well. On Mattos he found the case closer but concluded the officers acted reasonably given the danger from Troy and the close quarters of a domestic call, saying Aikala might have given more warning but was entitled to the latitude Graham gives split second judgments. Judge Silverman, joined by Judge Clifton, agreed that Brooks showed no violation, calling the tasing a humane way to remove a person who had conceded the police could remove her, but dissented in Mattos: disputed facts about whether her conduct was trivial required a trial, the law in August 2006 already prohibited disproportionate force for a trivial provocation, and if Mattos's version was credited the officer "dropped a nuclear bomb when a BB gun would have sufficed." Judge Schroeder concurred, emphasizing that neither woman posed any threat and that al-Kidd appeared to compel immunity.

applications.title: Count the cycles
applications.body: Three drive stun applications in less than one minute, with no time to recover and reconsider, was one of the two factors the court called overwhelmingly salient in Brooks. Each cycle is a separate use of force that needs its own reason.

applications.title: A known vulnerability raises the bar
applications.body: The officers knew Brooks was seven months pregnant and discussed where to apply the Taser before using it. The court treated that knowledge as weighing heavily against the reasonableness of the force.

applications.title: In the way is not fighting
applications.body: The court distinguished a failure to facilitate an arrest from active resistance. Jayzel Mattos stood between the officer and her husband, talked, and raised an arm to protect herself. That is not the active resistance that supports intermediate force.

applications.title: The danger of the call does not transfer to the victim
applications.body: Domestic calls are dangerous and the court said so. But the leeway given to officers entering a home to control a volatile scene does not extend to intermediate force on the non-threatening person they came to protect.

applications.title: Warn when you can
applications.body: Aikala fired without any warning. The court said the absence of a warning, when one was plausible, pushed the force far beyond the pale. A warning is a stated consequence and a chance to comply, not just a command.

applications.title: Posture
applications.body: A reasonable jury could find excessive force in both cases on the plaintiffs' facts, but the officers received qualified immunity on the federal claims because no court had held a Taser use unconstitutional in 2004 or 2006. Brooks's state assault and battery claims were allowed to go forward. Two partial dissents would have found the force reasonable.

quiz.q: Which two factors did the en banc court describe as overwhelmingly salient in finding that a jury could conclude the force on Brooks was excessive?
options: That she was speeding in a school zone and refused to sign
That the officers knew she was pregnant and considered it, and that she was tased three times in less than one minute
That she honked her horn and that the keys were in the ignition
That she was outnumbered and that it was daylight
quiz.teach: The court found her offenses minor, no immediate threat once the keys were removed, and some non-violent resistance. It then singled out the known pregnancy and the three rapid applications that left no time to recover and reconsider.

quiz.q: In Mattos, how did the court treat Jayzel's failure to move out of the way when Aikala announced the arrest?
options: As active resistance justifying intermediate force
As a failure to facilitate an arrest, which it distinguished from active resistance, noting she was trying to comply with another officer's request to step outside
quiz.teach: The court drew an express distinction between failing to facilitate an arrest and actively resisting it, and found this factor weighed in Jayzel's favor. Her only contact with the officer was defensive.

quiz.q: Why were the officers in both cases granted qualified immunity on the section 1983 claims?
options: Because the court found the force reasonable
Because Tasers are not a use of force

Because in 2004 and 2006 no Supreme Court or Ninth Circuit decision addressed Taser use and the only circuit Taser cases had rejected excessive force claims, so the violation was not clearly established beyond debate
Because the plaintiffs were convicted of resisting arrest
quiz.teach: Applying Ashcroft v. al-Kidd, the court held the existing precedent (Russo, Hinton and Draper, all rejecting Taser claims) did not place the question beyond debate and that the violations were not so obvious that Graham alone gave notice. The court followed the same approach it took in Bryan.
